# My question and the 1970 data

Based on the feedback, I focus on **1970**, the year I analysed in
Homework 2. I rerun the exploratory analysis, model comparison, diagnostics
and grid predictions for this year. The aim is to predict annual rainfall
and give an approximate 95% prediction interval at each supplied grid point.

Kriging combines a broad mean pattern with a correction based on nearby
residuals. I use maximum likelihood to estimate each model and
cross-validation to compare its predictions and intervals.

```{r load-1970}
source_data <- new.env()
invisible(load("data/RainData.RData", envir = source_data))
dat <- subset(source_data$dati, anno == 1970)
grid <- source_data$grid
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(grid,
  rbind(source_data$Basquota32, source_data$Calabriaquota32),
  check.attributes = FALSE)))

# I keep all three stations and correct only their regional labels.
region_fix <- c("4085" = "Basilicata", "4086" = "Basilicata",
                "4367" = "Calabria")
dat$Nome_Regione <- as.character(dat$Nome_Regione)
i <- dat$ID %in% as.numeric(names(region_fix))
dat$Nome_Regione[i] <- unname(region_fix[as.character(dat$ID[i])])
stopifnot(nrow(dat) == 189, all(dat$anno == 1970), !anyNA(dat),
  !anyNA(grid), all(dat$totanno > 0), !anyDuplicated(dat$ID),
  !anyDuplicated(dat[c("XUTM", "YUTM")]),
  !anyDuplicated(grid[c("XUTM", "YUTM")]))

add_coordinates <- function(d) {
  d$x <- d$XUTM/1000
  d$y <- d$YUTM/1000
  d$east <- (d$x-1100)/100
  d$north <- (d$y-4400)/100
  d$elev <- d$Quota/1000
  d
}
dat <- add_coordinates(dat)
grid <- add_coordinates(grid)
dat$rain <- dat$totanno
knitr::kable(data.frame(Stations = nrow(dat), Grid_points = nrow(grid),
  Mean_mm = mean(dat$rain), SD_mm = sd(dat$rain),
  Min_mm = min(dat$rain), Max_mm = max(dat$rain)), digits = 1)
```

I retain all **189 observations** and the supplied **1,005-point land grid**.
The original data file is unchanged. The matching grid is inside
`RainData.RData`; the separately supplied `AllGrids.RData` contains marine
data and is not used here. Only 1970 enters the analysis below.

As in Homework 2, I interpret rainfall as **mm**, elevation as **m**, and
the supplied projected coordinates as **m**. The file lacks complete unit
and coordinate-system metadata, so these remain assumptions. Distances use
the common supplied coordinates divided by 1,000, in km. I do not assign an
unverified EPSG code. The fixed centring and scaling of the trend covariates
also apply inside validation folds.

Elevation is available at both the stations and the grid. I use it as an
environmental predictor, with coordinates as possible additional trend
terms. Latitude and longitude repeat location information. Regional labels
describe the stations, but no corresponding regional factor is supplied
for the grid.

# Exploratory analysis

## Locations and observed rainfall

```{r map-tools}
draw_outlines <- function() {
  lines(source_data$Bas$XUTM/1000, source_data$Bas$YUTM/1000,
        col = "grey45", lwd = 0.7)
  lines(source_data$Cal$XUTM/1000, source_data$Cal$YUTM/1000,
        col = "grey45", lwd = 0.7)
}
map_frame <- function(title) {
  plot(grid$x, grid$y, type = "n", asp = 1,
    xlim = range(c(grid$x, dat$x)), ylim = range(c(grid$y, dat$y)),
    xlab = "Easting (km)", ylab = "Northing (km)", main = title)
  draw_outlines()
}
colour_key <- function(breaks, colours) {
  legend("bottomleft",
    paste(head(breaks, -1), tail(breaks, -1), sep = " to "),
    fill = colours, title = "mm", bty = "n", cex = 0.75)
}
```

```{r station-map, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 0.5))
map_frame("Stations, 1970")
region_col <- c(Basilicata = "#377EB8", Calabria = "#E69F00")
points(dat$x, dat$y, pch = 19, cex = 0.55,
       col = region_col[dat$Nome_Regione])
i <- match(as.numeric(names(region_fix)), dat$ID)
points(dat$x[i], dat$y[i], pch = 1, cex = 1.5)
text(dat$x[i], dat$y[i], dat$ID[i], pos = c(2, 4, 2), cex = 0.65)
legend("bottomleft", names(region_col), col = region_col,
       pch = 19, bty = "n", cex = 0.75)
map_frame("Observed rainfall, 1970")
breaks <- pretty(range(dat$rain), n = 5)
colours <- hcl.colors(length(breaks)-1, "YlGnBu", rev = TRUE)
points(dat$x, dat$y, pch = 19, cex = 0.65,
       col = colours[cut(dat$rain, breaks, include.lowest = TRUE)])
colour_key(breaks, colours)
```

The sampling region is elongated and the stations are unevenly spaced.
There are wetter and drier groups of stations, so a constant mean is not
an obvious description of the whole region. A visible pattern alone does
not separate a spatial trend from residual spatial dependence.

## Trend and Gaussianity

```{r covariate-plots, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(3.5, 4, 2, 0.5))
for (v in c("Quota", "x", "y")) {
  label <- c(Quota = "Elevation (m)", x = "Easting (km)",
             y = "Northing (km)")[v]
  plot(dat[[v]], dat$rain, pch = 19, cex = 0.5, col = "#267A8A",
       xlab = label, ylab = "Rainfall (mm)")
  lines(lowess(dat[[v]], dat$rain), col = "#C45A33", lwd = 1.5)
}
hist(dat$rain, breaks = "FD", col = "#B9DCE5", border = "white",
     main = "Rainfall distribution", xlab = "Rainfall (mm)")
```

Rainfall is positively associated with elevation: the correlation is
**`r fmt(cor(dat$rain, dat$Quota), 2)`**. The coordinate plots also show
broad geographical variation, especially lower rainfall towards the east.
This supports comparing an elevation trend
with an elevation-plus-coordinate trend. The association is descriptive;
it is not a causal estimate of the effect of elevation.

```{r gaussianity, fig.width=9, fig.height=3}
raw_lm <- lm(rain ~ elev + east + north, data = dat)
log_lm <- lm(log(rain) ~ elev + east + north, data = dat)
skewness <- function(z) mean((z-mean(z))^3)/mean((z-mean(z))^2)^1.5
distribution_check <- data.frame(
  Quantity = c("Raw rainfall", "Raw trend residuals", "Log trend residuals"),
  Skewness = c(skewness(dat$rain), skewness(resid(raw_lm)),
               skewness(resid(log_lm))))
knitr::kable(distribution_check, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 0.5))
z <- list(dat$rain, resid(raw_lm), resid(log_lm))
for (j in 1:3) {
  qqnorm(z[[j]], main = distribution_check$Quantity[j],
         pch = 19, cex = 0.45)
  qqline(z[[j]], col = "#C45A33")
}
```

The raw rainfall and raw-scale trend residuals have a right tail. Removing
the trend alone does not remove that asymmetry. The log-scale residuals
are more balanced and closer to a normal Q–Q line. This supports considering
a log transformation, although it does not prove a joint Gaussian model.
I keep both response scales in the predictive comparison. Any selected log
transformation will be used consistently in fitting, diagnostics and prediction.

# Model comparison by cross-validation

## Candidates and selection rule

For 1970 I model
\[
T\{Y(s)\}=X(s)\beta+w(s)+\epsilon(s),
\]
where $T$ is either the identity or the natural logarithm. The trend
$X(s)\beta$ describes the broad pattern; $w(s)$ is the remaining spatial
process; and $\epsilon(s)$ has variance $\tau^2$, the nugget. The nugget
allows measurement error or small-scale variation. I assume stationary,
isotropic residual covariance, and check that approximation later.

I compare two trends and three covariance families on each response scale:
**12 candidates**. The exponential allows a rougher field; the spherical
has a finite range; and Matérn with fixed $\kappa=1.5$ allows a smoother
field. Matérn $\kappa=0.5$ equals the exponential, so it would be redundant.

```{r candidates}
trends <- list(Elevation = ~elev,
               Elevation_xy = ~elev + east + north)
candidates <- expand.grid(Scale = c("Raw", "Log"),
  Trend = names(trends),
  Covariance = c("exponential", "spherical", "matern"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
candidates$Model <- seq_len(nrow(candidates))
```

I use the same five folds for every candidate. Each model is fitted by
**maximum likelihood using only training stations**, then predicts the
held-out stations. No other year enters these fits. The fixed seed keeps
the 1970 split reproducible. The analysis below is rerun without a cache.

Since uncertainty intervals are central to this homework, I select the
lowest mean **95% Interval Score**, using RMSE to break an exact tie:
\[
IS_{0.05}(l,u;y)=(u-l)+40(l-y)1(y<l)+40(y-u)1(y>u).
\]
It penalises unnecessary width and observations outside the interval.
It is a proper score for the central 95% predictive interval: its expected
value is minimised by the true 2.5% and 97.5% predictive quantiles. Lower
is better. Coverage alone can be inflated by making intervals too wide.
I also report RMSE for the predictive mean, coverage, width and bias, all
on the original rainfall scale. Scores are calculated at held-out stations;
there are no observed grid values with which to score grid predictions.

These are **selection scores**, not an independent assessment of the
whole selection procedure. Choosing the best of 12 models can make the
winning score optimistic. Random folds mainly assess interpolation among
the existing stations, not transfer to a large unsampled region.

## Fitting and prediction functions

I use two initial range values and retain the converged fit with the
higher likelihood. A failed start is counted. If neither start converges,
the analysis stops. Convergence and multiple starts are useful checks,
but cannot prove that a global maximum has been found.

```{r model-functions}
design <- function(d, trend) {
  geoR::trend.spatial(trends[[trend]], d)
}

fit_one <- function(d, candidate) {
  z <- if (candidate$Scale == "Log") log(d$rain) else d$rain
  g <- geoR::as.geodata(data.frame(x = d$x, y = d$y, z = z,
    elev = d$elev, east = d$east, north = d$north), covar.col = 4:6)
  X <- design(d, candidate$Trend)
  s2 <- mean(lm.fit(X, z)$residuals^2)
  fits <- lapply(c(20, 80), function(start) {
    tryCatch(geoR::likfit(g, trend = trends[[candidate$Trend]],
      cov.model = candidate$Covariance, kappa = 1.5, fix.kappa = TRUE,
      ini.cov.pars = c(0.8*s2, start), nugget = 0.2*s2,
      fix.nugget = FALSE, lambda = 1, fix.lambda = TRUE,
      lik.method = "ML", limits = geoR::pars.limits(phi = c(0.5, 1500)),
      messages = FALSE, control = list(maxit = 2000)),
      error = function(e) NULL)
  })
  ok <- vapply(fits, function(m) {
    !is.null(m) && is.finite(m$loglik) &&
      m$info.minimisation.function$convergence == 0
  }, logical(1))
  if (!any(ok)) stop("No converged fit for this candidate.")
  valid <- fits[ok]
  fit <- valid[[which.max(vapply(valid, function(m) m$loglik, numeric(1)))]]
  list(fit = fit, g = g, X = X, rejected = sum(!ok))
}

predict_one <- function(f, locations, candidate) {
  p <- geoR::krige.conv(f$g,
    locations = as.matrix(locations[c("x", "y")]),
    krige = geoR::krige.control(type.krige = "OK", obj.model = f$fit,
      trend.d = f$X, trend.l = design(locations, candidate$Trend),
      micro.scale = 0),
    output = geoR::output.control(signal = FALSE, messages = FALSE))
  mu <- p$predict
  v <- p$krige.var
  stopifnot(all(is.finite(mu)), all(is.finite(v)), all(v > 0))
  lower <- mu - qnorm(0.975)*sqrt(v)
  upper <- mu + qnorm(0.975)*sqrt(v)
  if (candidate$Scale == "Log") {
    answer <- data.frame(Mean = exp(mu + v/2),
                         Lower = exp(lower), Upper = exp(upper))
  } else {
    answer <- data.frame(Mean = mu, Lower = lower, Upper = upper)
  }
  answer$mu <- mu
  answer$variance <- v
  stopifnot(all(is.finite(as.matrix(answer))))
  answer
}

score_predictions <- function(y, p) {
  interval_score <- (p$Upper-p$Lower) +
    40*pmax(p$Lower-y, 0) + 40*pmax(y-p$Upper, 0)
  data.frame(RMSE = sqrt(mean((p$Mean-y)^2)),
    IS95 = mean(interval_score),
    Coverage = 100*mean(y >= p$Lower & y <= p$Upper),
    Width = mean(p$Upper-p$Lower), Bias = mean(p$Mean-y))
}
```

The external trend matrices make this **universal kriging**, even though
the `geoR` control option is named `OK`. I set `signal = FALSE` because
the target is annual rainfall at a new station-like location, including
the new observation's nugget variance.

## Rerunning the comparison for 1970

```{r cross-validation}
set.seed(2026 + 1970)
fold <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(dat)))
predictions <- scores <- vector("list", nrow(candidates))
rejected <- integer(nrow(candidates))
for (j in seq_len(nrow(candidates))) {
  p <- data.frame(Mean = rep(NA_real_, nrow(dat)), Lower = NA_real_,
                  Upper = NA_real_, mu = NA_real_, variance = NA_real_)
  for (k in 1:5) {
    test <- fold == k
    f <- fit_one(dat[!test, ], candidates[j, ])
    p[test, ] <- predict_one(f, dat[test, ], candidates[j, ])
    rejected[j] <- rejected[j] + f$rejected
  }
  predictions[[j]] <- p
  scores[[j]] <- score_predictions(dat$rain, p)
}
scores <- cbind(candidates, do.call(rbind, scores))
ranking <- order(scores$IS95, scores$RMSE)
best <- ranking[1]
runner_up <- ranking[2]
choice <- candidates[best, ]
knitr::kable(scores[ranking,
  c("Model", "Scale", "Trend", "Covariance", "IS95", "RMSE")],
  digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
```

For 1970 I select **`r choice$Scale` rainfall, an elevation trend and
`r choice$Covariance` covariance**. Its mean Interval Score is
**`r fmt(scores$IS95[best], 2)` mm** and RMSE is
**`r fmt(scores$RMSE[best], 2)` mm**. The second-best interval score is
**`r fmt(scores$IS95[runner_up], 2)` mm**, for model
**`r candidates$Model[runner_up]`**, the log-elevation Matérn model. The gap
is only **`r fmt(scores$IS95[runner_up]-scores$IS95[best], 2)` mm**, or about
**`r fmt(100*(scores$IS95[runner_up]/scores$IS95[best]-1), 2)`%**. I therefore
see the spherical model as a reasonable working choice, not strong evidence
that its shape is better than every alternative.

The response scale matters more here: log-model Interval Scores range from
**`r fmt(min(scores$IS95[scores$Scale == "Log"]))`** to
**`r fmt(max(scores$IS95[scores$Scale == "Log"]))` mm**, whereas raw-model
scores range from **`r fmt(min(scores$IS95[scores$Scale == "Raw"]))`** to
**`r fmt(max(scores$IS95[scores$Scale == "Raw"]))` mm**. This agrees with the
better-balanced log residuals in the exploratory plots. Adding east and
north coordinates does not improve the best score once elevation and
residual spatial covariance are included. A visible coordinate pattern
therefore does not automatically justify extra trend terms.

```{r chosen-scores}
chosen_scores <- scores[best, c("IS95", "RMSE", "Coverage", "Width", "Bias")]
knitr::kable(chosen_scores, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE)
cv <- predictions[[best]]
misses <- sum(dat$rain < cv$Lower | dat$rain > cv$Upper)
```

The intervals cover **`r fmt(chosen_scores$Coverage, 2)`%** of held-out
observations, with **`r misses` of `r nrow(dat)` observations outside**.
This is below the nominal 95%, so the intervals are not perfectly
calibrated. Their mean width is **`r fmt(chosen_scores$Width, 2)` mm**.
The Interval Score is larger than this width because it also penalises
misses. The mean prediction error is **`r fmt(chosen_scores$Bias, 2)` mm**;
positive values mean overprediction. These are results on one partition,
with overlapping training samples, rather than a formal independent
coverage test.

# The fitted model and its diagnostics

```{r final-fit}
final <- fit_one(dat, choice)
m <- final$fit
parameter_table <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c("Partial sill (log units squared)",
    "Nugget (log units squared)", "Range phi (km)", "Nugget share"),
  Estimate = c(m$cov.pars[1], m$nugget, m$cov.pars[2],
               m$nugget/(m$nugget+m$cov.pars[1])))
knitr::kable(parameter_table, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(data.frame(Term = colnames(model.matrix(trends[[choice$Trend]], dat)),
                        Coefficient = as.numeric(m$beta)),
             digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
range_bound <- m$cov.pars[2] < 0.51 | m$cov.pars[2] > 1499
stopifnot(m$info.minimisation.function$convergence == 0)
```

The selected spherical model has a finite residual-correlation range of
about **`r fmt(m$cov.pars[2])` km**. Its nugget is about
**`r fmt(100*m$nugget/(m$nugget+m$cov.pars[1]))`%** of the total residual
variance. This represents unstructured variation; it is not automatically
evidence of poor measurements. The variance parameters refer to **log
rainfall**, while the range still uses distances in km.

The fitted elevation coefficient corresponds to about
**`r fmt(100*(exp(m$beta[2]/10)-1), 2)`%** higher median rainfall per
100 m of elevation in the trend, holding the spatial residual component
fixed. It is an association within the model, not a causal effect.
The broader coordinate trend did not win the predictive comparison.

There were **`r sum(rejected)+final$rejected` rejected optimisation starts**
across validation and the final fit. The selected range is
**`r if (range_bound) "at a search boundary" else "away from the search boundaries"`**.
I choose the trend by prediction quality, not simply by obtaining the
smallest possible nugget.

## Variogram and directional checks

```{r variograms, fig.width=8, fig.height=3.7}
cutoff <- max(dist(final$g$coords))/2
breaks <- seq(0, cutoff, length.out = 13)
v_raw <- geoR::variog(final$g, breaks = breaks, trend = "cte",
                       messages = FALSE)
v_res <- geoR::variog(final$g, breaks = breaks,
  trend = trends[[choice$Trend]], messages = FALSE)
directions <- lapply(c(0, 45, 90, 135), function(a) {
  geoR::variog(final$g, breaks = breaks, trend = trends[[choice$Trend]],
    direction = a*pi/180, tolerance = pi/8, messages = FALSE)
})
h <- seq(0, cutoff, length.out = 200)
gamma <- m$nugget + m$cov.pars[1] -
  geoR::cov.spatial(h, cov.model = m$cov.model,
                    cov.pars = m$cov.pars, kappa = m$kappa)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 0.5))
plot(v_raw$u, v_raw$v, type = "b", pch = 1,
     ylim = range(c(v_raw$v, v_res$v, gamma)),
     xlab = "Distance (km)", ylab = "Semivariance (log scale)",
     main = "Trend and residual structure")
lines(v_res$u, v_res$v, type = "b", pch = 19, col = "#267A8A")
lines(h, gamma, col = "#C45A33", lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", c("Before detrending", "After detrending", "ML curve"),
       col = c("black", "#267A8A", "#C45A33"), lty = 1,
       cex = 0.7, bty = "n")
plot(v_res$u, v_res$v, type = "n",
     ylim = range(unlist(lapply(directions, function(v) v$v))),
     xlab = "Distance (km)", ylab = "Residual semivariance",
     main = "Directions after detrending")
for (j in 1:4) lines(directions[[j]]$u, directions[[j]]$v,
                     col = j, lty = j)
legend("topleft", c("0 degrees", "45 degrees", "90 degrees", "135 degrees"),
       col = 1:4, lty = 1:4, cex = 0.7, bty = "n")
knitr::kable(data.frame(Lag_km = v_res$u, Pairs = v_res$n,
                        Residual_semivariance = v_res$v),
             digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

Both empirical curves are on the **log scale**. I use 12 equal-width bins
up to **`r fmt(cutoff)` km**, half the largest station separation. Removing
the elevation trend lowers the longer-distance semivariance, but the
residual curve still rises at shorter distances. This supports modelling
residual spatial structure after allowing for the mean pattern.

The ML spherical curve is a broad approximation; it does not pass through
every empirical point. The fitted curve comes from the likelihood, not
from least-squares fitting of these plotted points. For nonzero distance,
$\gamma(h)=\tau^2+\sigma^2\{1-\rho(h)\}$; its value at the origin has a
nugget discontinuity.

The directional curves differ, particularly at longer distances. Some
directional bins have only
**`r min(unlist(lapply(directions, function(v) v$n)))` pairs**, so those
estimates are noisy. The elongated sampling region also affects which
directions and distances are represented. I treat stationarity and
isotropy as working assumptions, not conclusions proved by these plots.
An anisotropic model would be a possible extension, outside this candidate set.

## Held-out residuals

```{r held-out-diagnostics, fig.width=8, fig.height=3.6}
observed_scale <- if (choice$Scale == "Log") log(dat$rain) else dat$rain
standardised <- (observed_scale-cv$mu)/sqrt(cv$variance)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 0.5))
plot(dat$rain, cv$Mean, pch = 19, cex = 0.6, col = "#267A8A",
     xlab = "Observed rainfall (mm)", ylab = "Held-out mean (mm)",
     main = "Prediction check", asp = 1)
abline(0, 1, col = "#C45A33")
qqnorm(standardised, pch = 19, cex = 0.6,
       main = "Standardised held-out errors")
abline(0, 1, col = "#C45A33")
```

The predictions follow the broad rainfall pattern, with noticeable errors
at individual stations. Most standardised errors lie fairly close to the
normal reference line, but the tails are imperfect. Together with coverage
below 95%, this is a reason to call the intervals approximate. The held-out
errors share training observations, so I do not treat them as independent
data for a formal normality test.

# Prediction intervals: what they describe

The target is annual rainfall at an **unobserved location**, including
small-scale or measurement variation. These are **approximate pointwise
95% prediction intervals from a maximum-likelihood model**. They include
residual spatial variation, the nugget, and the universal-kriging correction
for estimating the trend coefficients. They treat the estimated covariance
parameters and selected model as fixed, so they omit that additional
uncertainty. They are not a simultaneous 95% band over all grid points.

In a Bayesian analysis, a **credible interval** describes posterior
uncertainty about a parameter, such as a regression coefficient, nugget,
partial sill or range. A **posterior predictive interval** describes an
unobserved value at a new location: it integrates parameter uncertainty
and remaining spatial variation, and includes the nugget when predicting
an observation rather than the latent field. Bayesian prediction maps
should therefore label such intervals *posterior predictive intervals*.
Here I have fitted no posterior distribution, so I use *prediction interval*
without the word *posterior*.

For the selected log model, if $m$ and $v$ are the kriging mean and
prediction-error variance on the log scale, I use
\[
\widehat{E(Y\mid\text{data})}=\exp(m+v/2),\qquad
[l,u]=[\exp(m-1.96\sqrt v),\ \exp(m+1.96\sqrt v)].
\]
The factor $v/2$ matters: $\exp(m)$ alone is a predictive median, not the
mean used for RMSE. I log rainfall explicitly and use `lambda = 1` in
`geoR` to avoid transforming twice. The same back-transformation is used
for held-out predictions and for the grid.

# The 1970 prediction maps

```{r grid-predictions}
mapped <- predict_one(final, grid, choice)
hull <- chull(dat$x, dat$y)
mapped$Outside_hull <- sp::point.in.polygon(
  grid$x, grid$y, dat$x[hull], dat$y[hull]) == 0
mapped$Outside_elevation <- grid$Quota < min(dat$Quota) |
                            grid$Quota > max(dat$Quota)
map_summary <- data.frame(Min_mean = min(mapped$Mean),
  Max_mean = max(mapped$Mean), Median_width = median(mapped$Upper-mapped$Lower),
  Outside_hull = sum(mapped$Outside_hull),
  Outside_elevation = sum(mapped$Outside_elevation))
knitr::kable(map_summary, digits = 1, row.names = FALSE)
```

Predicted means range from **`r fmt(min(mapped$Mean))` to
`r fmt(max(mapped$Mean))` mm**. The median interval width is
**`r fmt(median(mapped$Upper-mapped$Lower))` mm**. Higher predictions often
follow elevated interior areas, with local changes from the spatial
residual correction. I read these predictions together with their intervals.

There are **`r sum(mapped$Outside_hull)` points outside the station convex
hull** and **`r sum(mapped$Outside_elevation)` outside the observed elevation
range**; the groups can overlap. Station elevations range from
**`r min(dat$Quota)` to `r max(dat$Quota)` m**, while the grid reaches
**`r max(grid$Quota)` m**. High mountain predictions therefore rely partly
on extrapolating the trend. A point inside the geographical region can
still have an elevation outside the observed range.

```{r map-function}
draw_values <- function(values, breaks, title) {
  colours <- hcl.colors(length(breaks)-1, "YlGnBu", rev = TRUE)
  map_frame(title)
  points(grid$x, grid$y, pch = 15, cex = 0.55,
    col = colours[cut(values, breaks, include.lowest = TRUE)])
  draw_outlines()
  points(dat$x, dat$y, pch = 20, cex = 0.18)
  points(grid$x[mapped$Outside_hull], grid$y[mapped$Outside_hull],
         pch = 4, cex = 0.38, col = "grey25")
  points(grid$x[mapped$Outside_elevation], grid$y[mapped$Outside_elevation],
         pch = 2, cex = 0.48, col = "#B33A26")
  colour_key(breaks, colours)
}
```

```{r prediction-maps, fig.width=7.5, fig.height=8}
breaks <- pretty(range(mapped[c("Mean", "Lower", "Upper")]), n = 6)
width_breaks <- pretty(range(mapped$Upper-mapped$Lower), n = 6)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(3.5, 3.5, 2.3, 0.5), mgp = c(2, 0.6, 0))
draw_values(mapped$Mean, breaks, "Predicted mean, 1970")
draw_values(mapped$Lower, breaks, "Lower 95% prediction limit")
draw_values(mapped$Upper, breaks, "Upper 95% prediction limit")
draw_values(mapped$Upper-mapped$Lower, width_breaks, "95% interval width")
```

The mean and two limits share a colour scale; width has its own scale.
Black dots mark stations, crosses mark points outside their convex hull,
and red triangles mark elevation extrapolation. All supplied grid points
remain in the map. The log model keeps the prediction limits positive.

Wider intervals occur in parts of the northern edge and wetter interior.
On the log scale, the same standard error produces a larger width in mm
at a wetter location, so width is not simply a measure of station density.
The mapped intervals also cannot capture uncertainty from an incorrect
trend or covariance model, especially in extrapolation areas.

# What I conclude for 1970

The predictive comparison supports log rainfall, an elevation trend and
spherical residual covariance within this candidate set. Elevation accounts
for part of the broad pattern, while kriging uses the remaining spatial
association. The empirical and directional variograms still show features
that a simple isotropic model cannot capture exactly.

The selected model has mean **95% Interval Score
`r fmt(scores$IS95[best], 2)` mm**, **RMSE `r fmt(scores$RMSE[best], 2)` mm**,
and **coverage `r fmt(scores$Coverage[best], 2)`%**. The coverage and tail
diagnostics keep me cautious about interpreting the nominal 95% level.
Repeating validation splits or using spatially separated validation would
test stability more fully. Accounting for covariance-parameter uncertainty
would also be a useful next step. Those extensions are not performed here.

# Sources and software

I used the supplied lecture notes *Chapter1-2* for exploratory analysis and
variograms, *Chapter3-5* for likelihood kriging and its prediction target,
and *Chapter6-11*, Section 10.3, for the Interval Score. I use that score for
central predictive intervals here, while retaining a likelihood framework.
The `geoR` documentation supplies the function definitions and covariance
parameterisations.

```{r versions}
packages <- c("geoR", "sp", "knitr", "rmarkdown")
knitr::kable(data.frame(Component = c("R", packages),
  Version = c(as.character(getRversion()),
    vapply(packages, function(p) as.character(packageVersion(p)),
           character(1)))), row.names = FALSE)
```
